content: Linaclotide is indicated for the treatment of irritable bowel syndrome with constipation (IBS-C) at a dosage of 290 mcg taken orally once daily. For chronic idiopathic constipation (CIC), the recommended dosage is 145 mcg taken orally once daily, with a lower dose of 72 mcg daily being an option based on individual patient presentation. In pediatric patients aged 6 to 17 years with functional constipation (FC), a dose of 72 mcg taken orally once daily is recommended. Hypersensitivity reactions associated with linaclotide include anaphylaxis, angioedema, and rash (including hives or urticaria). Gastrointestinal adverse reactions may include hematochezia, nausea, and rectal hemorrhage. Linaclotide is contraindicated in patients under 2 years of age due to the risk of serious dehydration and in individuals with known or suspected mechanical gastrointestinal obstruction. Linaclotide and its active metabolite are minimally absorbed systemically following oral administration. Maternal use of linaclotide is not expected to result in fetal exposure. However, there is insufficient data on the use of linaclotide in pregnant women to determine any drug-associated risks for major birth defects or miscarriage. Linaclotide and its active metabolite were not detected in the milk of lactating women. In adults, plasma concentrations of linaclotide and its active metabolite were below the limit of quantification following multiple doses. Maternal use of linaclotide is not expected to expose breastfed infants to the drug or its active metabolite. There is no information on the effects of linaclotide on milk production. When prescribing linaclotide to breastfeeding mothers, clinicians should consider the developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding, the mother’s clinical need for the drug, and any potential adverse effects on the breastfed infant from the drug or the underlying maternal condition. No lactation studies in animals have been conducted, and it is unknown whether the negligible systemic absorption of linaclotide in adults results in clinically relevant exposure to breastfed infants. Linaclotide is a guanylate cyclase-C (GC-C) agonist. Activation of GC-C on the luminal surface of intestinal epithelial cells increases cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP), anion secretion, fluid secretion, and intestinal transit. The drug appears to act topically rather than systemically. Elevation of intracellular cGMP stimulates the secretion of chloride and bicarbonate into the intestinal lumen, primarily through activation of the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) ion channel, leading to increased intestinal fluid and accelerated transit. Systemic absorption of linaclotide is minimal. Plasma concentrations of linaclotide and its active metabolite are below the limit of quantification after oral doses of 145 mcg or 290 mcg. Linaclotide is metabolized within the gastrointestinal tract to its principal active metabolite by the loss of the terminal tyrosine moiety. Both linaclotide and its metabolite are proteolytically degraded within the intestinal lumen into smaller peptides and naturally occurring amino acids. Excretion occurs primarily via feces, with 3-5% of the parent compound and virtually 100% of the active metabolite being eliminated in this manner. Linaclotide should be taken on an empty stomach at least 30 minutes before the first meal of the day, at approximately the same time each day. The capsule should be swallowed whole and not chewed or crushed. The medication should be stored at 25°C (77°F), with permissible temperature excursions between 15-30°C (59-86°F). It must be kept in its original container, not subdivided or repackaged, and protected from moisture. The desiccant should not be removed from the container.
